title: Testing Async Thunks
description: Learn how to write tests for Redux async thunks including mocking API calls and testing pending/fulfilled/rejected states.

data.text: Real applications don't exist in isolation. They communicate with APIs, databases, and external services. Testing this async behavior requires different techniques than testing synchronous reducers. You need to mock API calls, control timing, and verify that your async thunks handle success and failure correctly.
This lesson covers testing async thunks using Jest's mocking capabilities and testing library utilities to ensure your async logic works correctly under various conditions.

Before testing, let's review how async thunks work. An async thunk dispatches three actions: **pending** (when started), **fulfilled** (on success), and **rejected** (on error). Your tests should verify each of these state transitions.

data.caption: Async thunk lifecycle
data.definition:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: async thunk dispatched
    Pending --> Fulfilled: API returns success
    Pending --> Rejected: API throws error
    Fulfilled --> [*]
    Rejected --> [*]

data.text: The simplest way to mock API calls is using `jest.fn()`. You can mock entire modules with `jest.mock()` or create mock functions for specific API calls.

data.caption: Testing async thunks flow
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Create mock API] --> B[Dispatch thunk]
    B --> C[Mock returns data]
    C --> D[Wait for completion]
    D --> E[Assert on store state]
    D --> F[Assert on dispatched actions]

data.text: When testing async operations, you need to wait for them to complete before making assertions. `@testing-library/react` provides `waitFor` which polls until the expectation passes or times out.

data.title: Using waitFor
data.content: Waiting for async operations in component tests

data.text: Redux Toolkit generates action creators for each phase of an async thunk. You can test that the correct actions are dispatched by capturing actions using `configureStore` with a custom middleware.

data.title: Testing Dispatched Actions
data.content: Verifying all three thunk phases dispatch correctly

data.text: Real apps often make multiple requests simultaneously. You should test that your reducers handle race conditions correctly, such as when an earlier request completes after a later one.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use jest.fn() and jest.mock() to mock API calls
Use waitFor to wait for async operations in components
Test both success and error paths
Consider race conditions with concurrent requests
data.takeaway: Testing async thunks requires mocking external dependencies and verifying state transitions at each phase of the async operation.
